title: August and the Harbor
premise: In the autumn of 1918, Ansel Amberdale drives for suffragist Edith Marchmont, secretly reading her correspondence and memorizing what matters. When a census taker's probing question exposes a hidden lodger — a German-born dockworker named Konrad to whom Ansel once promised safe passage — Ansel is caught between the state's machinery, Edith's cause, and their own conscience. As armistice rumors swirl and never quite arrive, Ansel smuggles Konrad toward the harbor through a city turning on its 'enemies,' discovering that belonging is something you carry, not something you're granted. The book ends with the armistice signed but uncelebrated: Konrad gone to sea on a neutral tramp steamer, Ansel keeping his letters, and Edith choosing to shelter Ansel rather than report them.
about_author: Paloma Eriksen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime letters in coastal municipal collections. She writes from a converted pilot house overlooking a working harbor.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. We meet Ansel reading Edith Marchmont's letters by lamplight before delivering them, measuring each day by what fits in a coat pocket. The emotional beat is quiet complicity: Ansel loves the intimacy of other people's words and fears being caught inside them.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A census taker arrives at the Marchmont house and asks about everyone sleeping under its roof. Ansel lies about Konrad, the German-born dockworker hiding in the boathouse, and the lie lands wrong. Beat: dread arriving politely, with a clipboard.

chapters.title: A Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, with a flashback to 1913 when Ansel promised Konrad passage out if things ever turned. Now Konrad is declared enemy alien, and the promise has become contraband. Beat: the weight of old kindnesses re-priced as crimes.

chapters.title: Edith's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She discovers Ansel's secret readings and Konrad's existence, and must weigh the movement's survival against one person's safety. Beat: power examined from the inside — even righteous causes learn to count lives selectively.

chapters.title: The Census Taker Calls Again
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Mr. Pell returns with follow-up questions and a suspicion he enjoys too much; Ansel realizes the state doesn't need proof, only paperwork. Beat: paranoia sharpening into resolve — Ansel decides to move Konrad before the week ends.

chapters.title: Letters Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ansel confesses the letter-reading to Edith; she reveals she always knew, and that some replies were drafted to be intercepted. Beat: betrayal transmuted into strange trust — two keepers of secrets agreeing whose secrets matter.

chapters.title: The Harbor at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A failed first attempt: the neutral tramp steamer has been requisitioned, and Pell's men are watching the docks. Konrad nearly surrenders himself. Beat: hope receding like the tide, leaving the mud of what they owe each other exposed.

chapters.title: Rumors of Peace
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Armistice rumors sweep the city; crowds celebrate prematurely, then turn ugly against anyone foreign. Edith uses her public standing to misdirect a mob away from the boathouse. Beat: power briefly bent toward mercy, at real cost to her cause.

chapters.title: The Last Manifest
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Climax: Pell corners Ansel at the harbor with the falsified manifest in hand. Ansel trades the one thing that can save themselves — Edith's most incriminating letter — for Konrad's berth on a departing collier. Beat: sacrifice as arithmetic finally done honestly.

chapters.title: After the Guns
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, months later. The armistice is signed; bells ring for a peace that feels borrowed. Konrad's first letter arrives from a port Ansel won't name, and Edith burns it unread, handing back the envelope sealed. Beat: belonging restored in miniature — a promise kept, a home chosen, not granted.
